```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,

```

```{r setup}
library(genmetalite)
set.seed(2026)
```

## The problem

You want the coefficients of a regression of `y` on `x1`, `x2` and `x3`. No
single study measured all three. Study 1 has `x1` and `x2`; study 2 has `x1` and
`x3`; study 3 has `x2` and `x3`. Separately, a large reference sample — a
national survey, a biobank — measured all three covariates but has no outcome.

If the covariates were independent, you could simply meta-analyse the
coefficients as reported. They are not: omitting `x3` from study 1 biases its
`x2` coefficient, because `x3` is correlated with `x2` and its effect gets
absorbed. Each study is estimating a different marginal effect, so averaging
them averages incompatible quantities.

## Simulating the situation

```{r}
make_pop <- function(n) {
  x1 <- rnorm(n)
  x2 <- 0.6 * x1 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.8)
  x3 <- 0.4 * x2 + rnorm(n)
  data.frame(x1 = x1, x2 = x2, x3 = x3)
}

beta <- c(x1 = 1, x2 = -0.5, x3 = 0.3)

make_study <- function(n, drop) {
  d <- make_pop(n)
  d$y <- as.numeric(2 + as.matrix(d) %*% beta + rnorm(n))
  d[, setdiff(names(d), drop), drop = FALSE]
}

ref <- make_pop(20000)
cohorts <- list(
  make_study(1500, "x3"),
  make_study(1500, "x2"),
  make_study(1500, "x1")
)

vapply(cohorts, function(d) paste(setdiff(names(d), "y"), collapse = ", "),
  character(1)
)
```

Note the conventions: the outcome is called `y` in every cohort, and the
reference data have no outcome column at all.

## Fitting

```{r}
fit <- calc_linear_beta(cohort_data = cohorts, ref_data = ref)
summary(fit)
```

The `estimate` column is close to the truth. The `ivw.estimate` column — plain
inverse-variance weighted meta-analysis of the same reduced models — is not:

```{r}
rbind(
  truth = beta,
  genmetalite = round(fit$linear_est$beta, 3),
  IVW = round(fit$IVW_est$beta[names(beta)], 3)
)
```

## Running the pipeline by hand

`calc_linear_beta()` is a wrapper around three steps you can run yourself, which
is useful when studies cannot share individual-level data.

### 1. Fit the reduced models

```{r}
reduced <- lapply(cohorts, function(d) {
  run_regression(
    y = d$y,
    X_s = d[, setdiff(names(d), "y"), drop = FALSE],
    dgp = "linear"
  )
})
reduced[[1]]
```

Each element carries the coefficients, a robust variance matrix and the
empirical covariance of that study's own covariates. That is all a collaborating
site needs to send you — no individual-level rows.

If a site has already fitted the model, `as_reduced_model()` converts an `lm` or
`glm` object into the same structure:

```{r}
fit_lm <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = cohorts[[1]])
as_reduced_model(fit_lm)$theta_hat_s
```

### 2. Assemble the covariances

```{r}
sig <- make_sigma_X_ls(
  n_cohorts = 3,
  reg_out = reduced,
  ref_data = ref,
  cohort_data = cohorts,
  cov_p_type = "partitioned"
)
round(sig$sigma_X_ls[[1]], 3)
```

Study 1 measured `x1` and `x2`, so that block is its own covariance. Everything
touching `x3` is borrowed from the reference population.

### 3. Map and pool

```{r}
est <- linear_estimate(
  n_cohorts = 3,
  reg_out = reduced,
  sigma_X_ls = sig$sigma_X_ls,
  cov_cohort_X_s_ls = sig$cov_cohort_X_s_ls,
  cohort_data = cohorts,
  ref_pop_dummy = sig$ref_pop_dummy
)
est
```

The design maps show what the mapping is doing:

```{r}
round(est$A[[1]], 3)
```

Study 1's `x1` and `x2` coefficients map to themselves (the identity block), and
the third column is the regression of the missing `x3` on the two observed
covariates — the path through which `x3`'s effect leaked into study 1's
estimates.

## Where the standard errors come from

```{r}
data.frame(
  naive = round(sqrt(diag(est$M)), 4),
  full = round(sqrt(diag(est$var)), 4)
)
```

`M` is the GLS variance you would get if the mapping `A_s` were known exactly.
The full variance adds the cost of estimating it: an `O(1/n_ref)` term from the
finite reference sample, and — under `cov_p_type = "partitioned"` — an
`O(1/n_s)` term because each study's own covariance block is estimated on the
same rows as its coefficients.

Both extra terms need individual-level data. Without the reference rows:

```{r}
est_no_ref <- suppressWarnings(linear_estimate(
  n_cohorts = 3,
  reg_out = reduced,
  sigma_X_ls = sig$sigma_X_ls,
  cov_cohort_X_s_ls = sig$cov_cohort_X_s_ls,
  cohort_data = NULL,
  ref_pop_dummy = NULL
))
identical(unname(est_no_ref$var), unname(est_no_ref$M))
```

You get a warning and the naive variance. That is fine when the reference sample
is enormous relative to the studies, and too small otherwise.

## Choosing `cov_p_type`

```{r}
fit_part <- calc_linear_beta(
  cohort_data = cohorts, ref_data = ref, cov_p_type = "partitioned"
)
fit_ref <- calc_linear_beta(
  cohort_data = cohorts, ref_data = ref, cov_p_type = "reference"
)

rbind(
  partitioned = round(fit_part$linear_est$beta, 3),
  reference = round(fit_ref$linear_est$beta, 3),
  truth = beta
)
```

Here the studies and the reference are drawn from the same population, so the
two agree. They diverge when a study's covariate distribution genuinely differs
from the reference — which is exactly when you should think about reweighting.

## Reweighting the reference

If a study's covariate distribution differs from the reference population, the
borrowed cross-moments describe the wrong population. Reweight first:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ebal", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_w <- calc_linear_beta(
  cohort_data = cohorts,
  ref_data = ref,
  weighting.vars = c("x1", "x2", "x3"),
  weighting.method = "ebal"
)
round(fit_w$linear_est$beta, 3)
```

`ebal_weights()` matches the requested moments exactly while keeping the weights
tightly dispersed; `ipw_weights()` fits a logistic membership model and returns
odds weights, with no extra package dependency. Either can be called directly if
you want to inspect the weights before using them:

```{r}
w <- ipw_weights(cohorts[[1]][, c("x1", "x2")], ref[, c("x1", "x2")])
summary(w$weights)
```

Weights are treated as fixed in the variance calculation. Estimating them
contributes a further influence-function term that is not included, so standard
errors under reweighting are mildly anti-conservative. A joint bootstrap over
study and reference rows is the recommended check.

## Constraining coefficients to zero

Sometimes you want to shrink a coefficient to exactly zero — because theory says
it is null, or because you want a nested model for comparison:

```{r}
fit_c <- calc_linear_beta(
  cohort_data = cohorts, ref_data = ref, constr_vars = "x3"
)
round(fit_c$linear_est$beta, 4)
```

The constrained variance sandwiches the full influence-function variance by the
projector, which is valid when the constraint really does hold in the
population.

## Categorical covariates

Factors are expanded with `model.matrix()`, so a factor `edu` with levels
`1, 2, 3` becomes `edu2` and `edu3`. The reference data and the cohorts must use
the same levels, or the dummy names will not line up:

```{r}
n <- 4000
make_pop2 <- function(n) {
  data.frame(
    age = rnorm(n),
    edu = factor(sample(1:3, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.5, .3, .2)))
  )
}
b2 <- c(age = 0.8, edu2 = -0.4, edu3 = 0.6)

ref2 <- make_pop2(n)
mk2 <- function(n, drop) {
  d <- make_pop2(n)
  X <- model.matrix(~., d)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
  d$y <- as.numeric(1 + X %*% b2 + rnorm(n))
  d[, setdiff(names(d), drop), drop = FALSE]
}
cohorts2 <- list(mk2(2000, "edu"), mk2(2000, character(0)))

fit2 <- calc_linear_beta(cohort_data = cohorts2, ref_data = ref2)
rbind(estimate = round(fit2$linear_est$beta, 3), truth = b2)
```

`check_vars()` will tell you in advance if a cohort has a level the reference
population lacks:

```{r}
check_vars(
  data.frame(g = factor(c("a", "b"))),
  data.frame(g = factor(c("a", "c")))
)
```

## Survey reference populations

A reference population is a *sample*, and how it was drawn matters. `ref_data`
accepts a `survey.design` object, or a `ref_design()` you build yourself:

```{r}
set.seed(77)
n_str <- 8; n_psu <- 5; m <- 60
N <- n_str * n_psu * m
psu <- rep(seq_len(n_str * n_psu), each = m)
strata <- rep(seq_len(n_str), each = n_psu * m)
u <- rnorm(n_str * n_psu, sd = 0.9)[psu]   # PSU-level clustering
sx1 <- u + rnorm(N)
sx2 <- 0.6 * sx1 + rnorm(N, sd = 0.8)
sx3 <- 0.4 * sx2 + rnorm(N)
svy_ref <- ref_design(
  data.frame(x1 = sx1, x2 = sx2, x3 = sx3),
  weights = exp(rnorm(N, 0, 0.4)) * 100,
  strata  = strata,
  psu     = psu
)
svy_ref
```

```{r}
fit_svy <- calc_linear_beta(cohort_data = cohorts, ref_data = svy_ref)
fit_svy$linear_est$design_df
```

The design changes the variance without touching the point estimate — `Sigma`
depends on the weights, the design enters only the variance:

```{r}
weights_only <- calc_linear_beta(
  cohort_data = cohorts,
  ref_data = ref_design(svy_ref$data, weights = svy_ref$weights)
)
rbind(
  `weights only` = round(sqrt(diag(weights_only$linear_est$var)), 4),
  `with design`  = round(sqrt(diag(fit_svy$linear_est$var)), 4)
)
identical(
  round(weights_only$linear_est$beta, 12),
  round(fit_svy$linear_est$beta, 12)
)
```

Clustering inflates the reference term, as it should. With `design_df` this
small, build confidence intervals from a *t* distribution rather than a normal:

```{r}
b  <- fit_svy$linear_est$beta
se <- sqrt(diag(fit_svy$linear_est$var))
crit <- qt(0.975, fit_svy$linear_est$design_df)
round(cbind(estimate = b, lower = b - crit * se, upper = b + crit * se), 3)
```

If you use the survey package, pass the design object straight in and skip the
manual construction:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("survey", quietly = TRUE)}
des <- survey::svydesign(
  id = ~psu, strata = ~strata, weights = ~w,
  data = cbind(svy_ref$data, psu = psu, strata = strata, w = svy_ref$weights),
  nest = TRUE
)
fit_des <- calc_linear_beta(cohort_data = cohorts, ref_data = des)
all.equal(fit_des$linear_est$var, fit_svy$linear_est$var)
```

The design's `variables` slot carries `psu`, `strata` and `w` alongside the
covariates; only the covariates the studies use enter the model, so there is no
need to strip them first.

For NHANES the call is the same shape:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
des <- survey::svydesign(
  id = ~SDMVPSU, strata = ~SDMVSTRA, weights = ~WTMEC2YR,
  data = nhanes, nest = TRUE
)
fit <- calc_linear_beta(cohort_data = cohorts, ref_data = des)
```

Finite population corrections are ignored, giving the with-replacement variance
NCHS recommends. Calibrated or post-stratified designs get a warning and a
conservative variance, since those adjustments are not propagated.

### Reweighting a survey reference

Reweighting composes with the design. The sampling weights become the base
weights of the balancing problem, so each cohort ends up with one weight vector
carrying both:

```{r}
fit_both <- calc_linear_beta(
  cohort_data = cohorts,
  ref_data = svy_ref,
  weighting.vars = c("x1", "x2", "x3"),
  weighting.method = "ebal"
)

## Cohort 1 measured x1 and x2; both are matched exactly.
w1 <- fit_both$ref_weights[[1]]
rbind(
  `weighted reference` = c(
    x1 = weighted.mean(svy_ref$data$x1, w1),
    x2 = weighted.mean(svy_ref$data$x2, w1)
  ),
  cohort = c(x1 = mean(cohorts[[1]]$x1), x2 = mean(cohorts[[1]]$x2))
)
```

The population total the survey weights represent survives the reweighting, and
each cohort gets its own vector:

```{r}
c(
  survey_total = sum(svy_ref$weights),
  cohort1 = sum(fit_both$ref_weights[[1]]),
  cohort2 = sum(fit_both$ref_weights[[2]])
)
fit_both$linear_est$design_df
```

Per-cohort weights and a shared design coexist because the per-cohort influence
contributions are summed *before* the design is applied. The cohorts are all
reweighting the same reference rows, so their contributions are correlated;
summing first keeps that, whereas adding per-cohort variances would understate
it.

Weights are still treated as fixed. Estimating them contributes a further
influence-function term that is not included, so standard errors under
reweighting are mildly anti-conservative.

## When a study is itself a complex sample

The reference design is handled for you. A *study's* design is not:
`linear_estimate()` takes each study's coefficient covariance as given, and the
default sandwich assumes independent rows. For a clustered cohort, fit the model
yourself and pass a cluster-robust matrix:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit_lm <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = cohort1)
rm1 <- as_reduced_model(
  fit_lm,
  vcov = function(f) sandwich::vcovCL(f, cluster = cohort1$psu)
)
```

In simulation, clustered cohorts fitted with the plain sandwich dropped 95%
interval coverage to about 0.89 even with the reference design handled
correctly, so this is worth getting right when it applies.

## Chaining fits

A pooled estimate can act as one study in a second round of pooling, which is
useful for combining consortia that have each run their own meta-analysis:

```{r}
rm_pooled <- as_reduced_model_genmetalite(fit, cov_X = cov(ref))
rm_pooled$theta_hat_s
```
